epithet: Amin al-Ummah (The Trustee of the Nation)
role: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
Commander of the Islamic conquest of Syria (Sham)
Amin al-Ummah — Trustee of the Nation
summary: Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA) was one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise and was given by the Prophet ﷺ the singular title Amin al-Ummah — the Trustee of the Nation. He led the Islamic conquest of Syria (Sham), bringing the entire Levant under Islamic governance within a few years. He died of plague in the Plague of Amwas, refusing to leave his soldiers in the afflicted land, and is buried in the Jordan Valley.
biography:
Abu Ubaydah Amir ibn Abdullah ibn al-Jarrah al-Fihri al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 583 CE into the Banu al-Harith ibn Fihr clan of Quraysh. He was among the earliest converts to Islam, accepting the faith on the same day as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Uthman ibn Affan (RA) — that is, in the very first days of the Prophet's ﷺ call. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra names him among the first group of eight who accepted Islam.

He was known among the Companions for his extraordinary physical appearance: tall, lean, slightly hunched, with a sparse beard and two front teeth missing — teeth he himself knocked out at the Battle of Uhud. At that battle, the Prophet ﷺ was wounded and metal rings from his helmet had pierced his cheeks. Abu Ubaydah removed them by gripping them with his teeth, pulling them out of the Prophet's ﷺ flesh one by one, losing a tooth each time. He did not flinch. This act of devoted service is preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

The Prophet ﷺ conferred upon him the title Amin al-Ummah: 'Every nation has its trustee, and the trustee of this nation is Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il al-Sahaba; Sahih Muslim, Kitab Fada'il al-Sahaba). This title indicated a person of absolute integrity and trustworthiness — one in whose hands the affairs of the community were safe. The Prophet ﷺ used this characterization for no other Companion.

At the Battle of Badr (2 AH), Abu Ubaydah faced his own father, Abdullah ibn al-Jarrah, who fought on the side of the Quraysh. His father sought him out in battle. Abu Ubaydah initially withdrew, but his father persisted. In the end, Abu Ubaydah struck his father. This intensely difficult act was noted by the Companions and later referenced in the Quran's affirmation that faith can override the ties of kinship when it comes to defending the truth (Quran 58:22 in the context of companions not taking enemies of Allah as allies). Al-Dhahabi records this in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala'.

He participated in all the major battles: Uhud, al-Khandaq, Khaybar, the conquest of Makkah, Hunayn, and Tabuk. He was sent by the Prophet ﷺ on numerous military expeditions as commander. After the Prophet's ﷺ death, at the gathering of Saqifah where the early Muslims debated succession, Abu Bakr himself offered the caliphate to either Umar ibn al-Khattab or Abu Ubaydah, considering them both most qualified. Both declined, insisting that Abu Bakr was the right choice.

Under Abu Bakr and then Umar (RA), Abu Ubaydah became the supreme commander of the Islamic armies in Syria (Sham). He replaced Khalid ibn al-Walid as the overall commander in Syria on Umar's instruction — a transition that Khalid accepted with admirable grace. Under Abu Ubaydah's command, the key battles of Ajnadayn (13 AH), Marj al-Suffar, and the decisive Battle of Yarmouk (15 AH) were fought. Following Yarmouk, the Byzantine forces withdrew and city after city fell: Damascus, Homs, Aleppo, Antioch, and Jerusalem. Umar (RA) personally came to Jerusalem to receive the keys of the city from the Patriarch Sophronius, and Abu Ubaydah was at his side.

In 18 AH (639 CE), the Plague of Amwas (Plague of Emmaus) swept through Syria, killing tens of thousands including many senior Companions and Muslim soldiers. Umar wrote to Abu Ubaydah commanding him to leave the infected area. Abu Ubaydah refused, writing back that he was with his soldiers and would not desert them. The plague took him. He died in Jabiya or in the Jordan Valley (near present-day Beit She'an), martyred by plague. Umar received the news in Madinah and wept, saying: 'Would that Abu Ubaydah were alive so I could make him my caliph.' He is buried in the Jordan Valley; his tomb is traditionally identified near the town of Dayr Alla.

notable_traits: Titled Amin al-Ummah by the Prophet ﷺ — a title of absolute trust given to no other
Self-sacrificing devotion: removed shrapnel from the Prophet's ﷺ wounds with his own teeth
Exceptional military command — conquered the entire Levant for Islam
Refused to abandon his soldiers during plague, choosing martyrdom over safety
Known for extreme humility despite his towering status among the Companions
